lead: Mobile computing means computing by a user who is moving. The device changes its point of attachment to the network. Keeping a session alive across that change is the hard part. This drives the design: a small battery-powered host, a fading radio link, and a fixed network tracking the user. UPI payments, IRCTC bookings, telemedicine and fleet tracking rest on this structure. This chapter gives the definition, characteristics, three-part structure and applications.
prereq: You need only the basic idea that data travels in packets with addresses; radio details come later in wireless LANs.

blocks.text: A mobile host is a computer that changes its point of attachment to the network. Keeping an open session alive across that change is the hard part. Mobility is the change of attachment; session continuity is the difficulty.
Wireless is not mobile. A desktop on Wi-Fi is wireless but never moves. A laptop plugged into a train's wired network keeps its session while the train moves, so it is mobile but not wireless.

items: Ubiquity: the user can compute from a bus, field or shop counter.
Location independence: the service follows the person; the address changes, the identity does not.
Adaptivity: the app adjusts to changing bandwidth, screen size and battery level.
Personalisation: one device, one owner, so content and alerts fit that person.
Connectivity: the user stays reachable, though the link drops in and out.
Constraint: small battery, modest CPU, small screen, metered data.

sections.h3: Structure: three parts and a middle layer

blocks.text: Every mobile system has three parts. The mobile host is the phone running the app. The radio access network is the first hop: a base station (BTS) for cellular, or a Wi-Fi access point. The fixed network is everything behind it plus servers holding data and business logic.

items: The app on the mobile host builds a small request.
The radio link carries it to the nearest base station or access point.
Mobile middleware handles location, security and sync.
The fixed network routes it to the server over IP.
The reply returns along the same chain.

blocks.text: Middleware does three jobs. Location management answers where the user is now, so a reply reaches a host that has moved; see Mobile IP. Security covers authentication, air encryption and safe key storage. Synchronisation reconciles a local copy with the server after a coverage gap.

Heavy work such as location lookup, authentication and sync reconciliation runs on servers in the network. Small client pieces such as the sync client and key store sit on the handset. When the host leaves a cell, handover moves it without dropping the session; see handover and location tracking.

items: UPI payments: a few-kilobyte request reaches the payment server; the bank replies in under a second.
IRCTC ticketing: seat availability and booking from a moving train; the app caches the last view.
Telemedicine: a doctor reads a patient's report from a village clinic over a weak link.
Fleet tracking: a truck's GPS position is pushed to a control room every few minutes.

blocks.text: For interactive cases (payments, ticketing, telemedicine), delay matters more than data rate. Fleet tracking is delay-tolerant but needs the position to arrive reliably.

examples.question: A UPI app on a phone sends a 2 KB request over a 4G link that runs at 5 Mbps. The one-way delay is 40 ms. Find the transmission time and total one-way time.
examples.answer: The request takes 3.2768 ms to push onto the link and 43.2768 ms total one way, so delay dominates, not data rate.
examples.check:
size_kb = 2
rate_mbps = 5
delay_ms = 40
bits = size_kb * 1024 * 8
tx_ms = bits / (rate_mbps * 1e6) * 1000
total_ms = tx_ms + delay_ms
print(bits)
print(tx_ms)
print(total_ms)

examples.question: A 4 KB photo uploads over a 10 Mbps link with a 30 ms one-way delay. Find the transmission time and total one-way time.
examples.answer: Transmission time is 3.2768 ms and total one-way time is 33.2768 ms.
examples.check:
bits = 4 * 1024 * 8
tx_ms = bits / (10 * 1e6) * 1000
print(bits)
print(tx_ms)
print(tx_ms + 30)

traps: Mobile and wireless are not synonyms. A laptop plugged into a train's wired network is mobile but not wireless; a desktop on Wi-Fi is wireless but not mobile.
Middleware is not the app. Heavy location lookup, security and sync reconciliation run as network services; small client pieces run on the handset.
Unit slip: here 1 KB means 1024 bytes, so 2 KB is 2048 bytes and 16 384 bits, not 16 000.
1 Mbps means 10⁶ bit/s, not 2²⁰ bit/s. This shifts transmission time by about 5%; total time barely moves because delay dominates.
Handover keeps a live session alive; location tracking finds an idle user. Examiners ask for both and mark them separately.

quiz.a: A computer that changes its point of attachment to the network.

quiz.q: Name any four characteristics of mobile computing.
quiz.a: Ubiquity, location independence, adaptivity, personalisation, connectivity, constrained device.

quiz.q: Why does a mobile system need middleware at all?
quiz.a: The host moves, so the network must map identity to a changing address (location), protect an open radio link (security), and reconcile a local copy with the server after a coverage gap (sync). Heavy work runs on servers; small client pieces sit on the handset.

quiz.q: A desktop PC connects by Wi-Fi. Is it a mobile host? Explain in one line.
quiz.a: No. It is wireless, but its point of attachment never changes at all.

quiz.q: A 4 KB upload crosses a 10 Mbps link with a 30 ms one-way delay. Compute the transmission time and total one-way time.
For a 2 KB request over 5 Mbps with 40 ms delay, transmission time is 3.2768 ms but total is 43.2768 ms. What does this say about designing mobile apps?
quiz.a: Delay, not bandwidth, sets the user's waiting time. Cut the number of round trips, cache and batch, rather than only shrinking the payload.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the middleware idea moved to the cloud: a push-notification service, token authentication server and sync engine do the three jobs. Edge computing puts the server nearer the base station so the 40 ms delay shrinks. 5G network slicing reserves a low-delay slice for payments and an ordinary slice for video. Search for mobile middleware, edge computing and network slicing.
